$comment: Declaration for scripts/verify/ref-expiry.sh — edit THIS, never the script's
internals, so there is exactly one place a number lives.
WHY THIS EXISTS. A full ref census on 2026-09-10 found 187 local branches and
106 remote branches in this clone. 184 of the local ones are STRICT ANCESTORS
of origin/dev — merged long ago, never deleted. They are not merely untidy:
they are camouflage. `git branch` becomes unreadable, and the one or two refs
that genuinely hold unlanded work are hidden inside 184 that do not.
The same census found eight git stashes accumulated since April, invisible to
any branch-based audit; one held ~4900 insertions. Nothing in this repo had
ever MEASURED ref accumulation, so it grew unopposed for months.
This gate is the meter. It is the age/expiry sibling of orphan-branch-drift.sh,
which asks a different question — 'does this content exist ONLY on this disk'.
A ref can be fully preserved on a remote (clean by that gate) and still be 200
days of dead weight (a finding here). Read the two together.
$why_trunk: The 2026-09-10 dev-trunk directive made `dev` the integration trunk, so `dev`
— not `main` — is where lane work actually lands and therefore the ref against
which 'has this landed?' is the right question. Overridable with CSQ_TRUNK for
a clone on a different model. The gate resolves origin/<trunk> first and falls
back to the local refs/heads/<trunk>; if NEITHER resolves it returns
UNDETERMINED rather than guessing, because a wrong trunk silently reclassifies
every landed ref as unlanded and vice versa.
$why_age: The threshold is on AGE, not on count, and it is deliberately generous.
A merged branch deleted the same week is normal hygiene and needs no gate. The
cost this number bounds is CAMOUFLAGE: how long a genuinely unlanded ref can
hide among landed ones before anyone would notice. 30 days is one calendar
month — long enough that no active branch is ever reported (the longest-lived
in-flight lane branch in this repo's history is well under a month), short
enough that the 184-branch backlog measured above could never have formed
silently: it would have fired in the first month and every month after.
The same number governs BOTH reported classes on purpose. A landed ref over 30
days is drainable; an UNLANDED ref over 30 days is the dangerous case, because
at that age nobody remembers what it holds. Using one bound keeps the question
'is this ref older than a month' single-valued.
$why_stash: Stashes get the same bound as branches because they are the same hazard with
worse visibility: `git branch`, `git log`, every PR view and every existing
audit in this repo is blind to refs/stash. The measured case is the argument —
eight stashes since April, one carrying ~4900 insertions, none surfaced by any
instrument. A stash is UNLANDED by construction (it was never committed), so
an old one is always the loud class, never the drainable one.
Same number as max_age_days rather than a second tunable to argue about: the
question is identical ('older than a month'), and two numbers for one question
$why_protected: NEVER reported and NEVER prunable, whatever their age or classification.
main and dev are the trunks themselves. `preserve/*` and `salvage/*` are the
names this repo's recovery discipline uses for refs deliberately parked
long-term — a salvage branch is SUPPOSED to be old and unlanded, so reporting
it would train the operator to ignore exactly the class of finding this gate
exists to make loud (instrument-discipline.md MUST-1: an override habit forms
because a gate cannot discriminate, not because it is frequent).
Matched as globs against the short ref name.
